1.title: the one at every doorway
1.hook: why Hindus begin everything with Ganesha, and the tusk he broke to keep writing
1.howItsDone: Hindus honor Ganesha first at pujas, weddings, housewarmings and new beginnings, keep his image near doorways and in shops, print his image or name at the top of invitations, and some write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before starting to write.

segments.voice: Every Hindu beginning starts with him, so this one does too. A small statue on a taxi dashboard. A picture above a shop counter. His name printed at the top of a wedding invitation, before anyone else's. Elephant head, round belly, one tusk broken. He sits wherever things start, and that's the clue to who he is.
screen: `EVERY BEGINNING STARTS WITH HIM.` → `DASHBOARDS. DOORWAYS. INVITATIONS.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Ganesha is gana plus isha: lord of the ganas, the attendants of the god Shiva. His best-known title is Vighnaharta. Vighna, an obstacle; harta, one who removes. The remover of obstacles. This is why Hindus begin everything with Ganesha: before a wedding, a puja, a new shop, a new home or an exam, you honor first the one who clears the way. And there's a story about him and a page. When the sage Vyasa was ready to give the world the Mahabharata, he needed a scribe who could keep up. Ganesha agreed, on one condition: Vyasa must never stop. Vyasa added his own: Ganesha must understand every verse before he wrote it down. So whenever Vyasa needed time, he spoke a verse so knotted that even Ganesha had to stop and think. And one telling says that when Ganesha's pen gave out, he snapped off his own tusk and kept writing. That's the broken tusk in his pictures. The remover of obstacles is also a god of wisdom and learning. So some people write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before they begin. Namah means a bow: a bow to Ganesha, before the work.
screen: `VIGHNAHARTA — REMOVER OF OBSTACLES.` · `HONORED FIRST, BEFORE ANY BEGINNING.` · `VYASA SPEAKS. GANESHA WRITES.` · `THE BROKEN TUSK.` · `SHRI GANESHAYA NAMAH.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Think of something you're beginning this week. If you pray, say shri ganeshaya namah once, under your breath, the way many Hindus do before they start. If you don't, rest a hand on the door or the notebook, and name what's in the way. Then breathe out, and begin.
Ganesha. Lord of the ganas, remover of obstacles, the one at the door. First word on your strand, and the first name.

2.title: the sound the universe hums
2.hook: a boy waits three days at Death's door and is given one word: om
2.tomorrow: the prayer you know by heart
2.howItsDone: Hindus chant om at the start of prayers, mantras and readings of scripture, often at the end too, and it is written as a single sacred sign, ॐ, in homes and temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesha, the one who goes first. Today, the sound that opens almost every Hindu prayer.

Om. A yoga class ends with it, and Hindu prayers begin with it. To see why, start with a boy who walked to Death's door. His father, in a temper, shouted at him: I give you to Death. So Nachiketa went. Death wasn't home. The boy waited at the door for three days without food, and when Death came back, ashamed to have kept a guest hungry, he offered him three wishes.
screen: `OM.` → `A BOY AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `THREE DAYS. THREE WISHES.`

segments.voice: For the third wish, Nachiketa asked the biggest question there is: what happens to us after we die? Death tried to talk him out of it. Take gold, he said. Horses, kingdoms, a long life. The boy said no: all of that ends. So Death taught him, and at the heart of the teaching was one word. The word every sacred text points to, Death said, is om. This syllable is Brahman: the one reality underneath everything. That's the big idea inside the sound. For Hindus, om isn't a hum. It's the name of the whole. Another short, old text says om is all of this, past, present and future, and hears four parts in it. A: waking, the world you can touch. U: dreaming. M: deep, dreamless sleep. And the fourth has no sound. It's the silence after the m runs out, and the text calls it the self, at peace. That's why prayers, mantras and readings of scripture begin with om. Before you ask for anything small, you name the whole. So the next time a room goes quiet before om, you'll know what's happening: everything is being named before anything is asked.
screen: `THE BIGGEST QUESTION.` · `OM IS BRAHMAN: THE WHOLE.` · `A, U, M — AND THE SILENCE.` · `NAME THE WHOLE FIRST.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Breathe in. Let it out as the sound, aloud or under your breath: a, u, m. Let the m run out on its own, then stay a second in the quiet after it. That quiet is the fourth part.
Om. A, u and m for waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and the silence after it for the fourth. Second word on your strand.

3.title: the prayer you know by heart
3.hook: a king who tried to take by force, and the prayer he's remembered for: asking only for a clear mind
3.carry: a prayer for a clear mind
3.howItsDone: Many Hindus say the Gayatri mantra at dawn, and often at dusk, sometimes a set number of times on a mala; it opens with om bhur bhuvah svah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: om, three sounds and a silence. Today it opens a prayer you might already know by heart.

Om bhur bhuvah svah. If you grew up in a Hindu home, there's a good chance you can say the rest without thinking. Maybe someone said it every morning. Maybe it played at every puja. Now the hard part: what does it ask for? Most people go quiet. The answer starts with a king who wanted something he couldn't take. First, a guess.
screen: `OM BHUR BHUVAH SVAH…` → `YOU CAN SAY IT.` → `WHAT DOES IT ASK FOR?`

segments.voice: Long ago a powerful king, Vishvamitra, stopped with his army at the forest home of the sage Vasishtha. The sage fed every soldier, thanks to a wondrous cow that could give anything. The king wanted her. He offered herds of cattle, gold, jewels. The sage said no. So the king tried to take her by force, and lost: his armies and his weapons failed against one sage with a staff. Stung, he gave up his throne and spent years in practice, failing and starting over, until at last even Vasishtha honored him as a great sage. Tradition names Vishvamitra as the seer of the prayer many Hindus say at dawn: the Gayatri. Listen to what it asks. Bhur bhuvah svah: earth, sky, and beyond. Tat savitur varenyam: that worthy light of Savitar, the sun that stirs the world awake. Bhargo devasya dhimahi: we meditate on that divine radiance. Dhiyo yo nah prachodayat: may it wake up and guide our minds. Not a cow. Not a kingdom. Not to win. A clear mind. The man who tried to take everything by force is remembered for a prayer that asks only to see. That's a mantra: man, to think, and tra, a tool. Some traditions teach the Gayatri at a coming-of-age ceremony; in many homes, everyone simply says it. If you grew up saying it without the meaning, you weren't doing it wrong. The night before an exam or a hard talk, it doesn't ask for the result. It asks for a mind that sees straight.
screen: `A KING WHO TRIED FORCE.` · `YEARS OF PRACTICE. THE GAYATRI.` · `MAY IT WAKE UP OUR MINDS.` · `MANTRA — A TOOL FOR THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Breathe in. As you breathe out, say the Gayatri once, slowly, out loud or in your head, or just its last line: dhiyo yo nah prachodayat, may it wake up and guide our minds. This time, mean the words.
Gayatri. The morning prayer for a clear mind, and a mantra: a tool for the mind. Third word on your strand.
Your line: a prayer for a clear mind. Next time you hear it, you'll know what's being asked. Day three.

4.title: the oldest hello
4.hook: on the morning of a war, a prince bows to the men he must fight; what namaste and pranam honor
4.carry: the light in me sees the light in you
4.howItsDone: Hindus greet one another with namaste or namaskar, palms pressed together at the chest and the head slightly bowed. The same gesture is made to elders, to guests and before images of the gods; in many families children touch an elder's feet (pranam), and the elder blesses them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Gayatri, a prayer for a clear mind. Today, a word you've said a thousand times as hello.

You've said it at the end of a yoga class, and you've probably heard it means the light in me sees the light in you. The word itself says something simpler. But the idea behind that line is real, and an old story shows it on a battlefield. First, a guess.

Namaste splits in two. Namas: a bow. Te: to you. I bow to you. Now the story. It's the morning of the great war in the Mahabharata. Two armies of cousins face each other, conches blowing. Suddenly the eldest Pandava brother, Yudhishthira, takes off his armor, lays down his weapons and walks alone toward the enemy. Both armies wonder if he's surrendering. He isn't. On the other side stand his great-uncle Bhishma and his teacher Drona, men who love him and are bound to fight against him. He bows at their feet and asks for their blessing. And Bhishma says: if you hadn't come, I would have wished you defeat. Because you came, I bless you. Why bow to the people you're about to fight? In the epic, it's dharma: you honor your elders and teachers, even across a battle line. And many teachers hear one of Hinduism's biggest ideas underneath. An old text says the light that shines above the heavens is the same light that is inside a person. Many Hindus call that inner self the atman, and see in it the same divine reality that runs through everything. Read that way, a bow isn't to someone's side, mood or rank. It's to what's in them. That's where the popular line comes from: the light in me sees the light in you. Not a translation; a reading, with a real source behind it. At home it goes further. When a kid touches a grandparent's feet, that's pranam, the same bow. And the elder's hand comes down on the child's head: a blessing given back, just as Bhishma gave his.
screen: `NAMAS — A BOW. TE — TO YOU.` · `YUDHISHTHIRA BOWS TO BHISHMA.` · `THE SAME LIGHT, INSIDE A PERSON.` · `A BLESSING, GIVEN BACK.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Palms together if you like, or just sit up straight. Breathe in. As you breathe out, tip your head slightly forward: the bow the word is named for. Nothing to feel, nothing to get right. Just the gesture, done once, on purpose.
Namaste. Word for word, I bow to you. Read deeper, the light in me sees the light in you. Fourth word on your strand.

5.title: light passed hand to hand
5.hook: fire that couldn't burn a blade of grass, and why Hindus offer a flame back to God
5.howItsDone: Arti is performed in temples and homes, often in the morning and evening: a lamp is waved before the image of God while a bell rings and a song is sung, and then the flame is brought to each person, who passes their hands over it and touches their eyes and forehead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: namaste, I bow to you, and the bow that touches an elder's feet. Today, the flame that comes around on a plate.

Evening at a temple, or a living room when the lamp comes out. A small flame sits on a metal plate, and someone moves it in slow circles before the shrine. A bell rings. People sing. Then the plate is carried around the room, and one by one, people pass their hands over the flame and bring their palms to their eyes and forehead. Why offer fire to God at all? An old story has an answer.
screen: `A FLAME ON A PLATE.` → `SLOW CIRCLES. A BELL.` → `WHY OFFER FIRE TO GOD?`

segments.voice: Arti: the waving of a lamp, the offering of light. The best-known song begins om jai jagadish hare: victory to you, lord of the world. Now the story, from one of the oldest Hindu texts. The gods once won a great victory and grew proud: we did this. Then a strange being appeared before them, and nobody knew who it was. They sent Agni, the god of fire. I can burn anything on earth, he boasted. The being set down a single blade of grass. Burn this. Agni rushed at it with everything he had, and couldn't burn it. The god of the wind went next: I can blow away anything. He couldn't move the grass. Then Indra, king of the gods, came near, and the being vanished. In its place stood a shining goddess, Uma, who told him: that was Brahman. The victory was Brahman's all along. Fire burns because of Brahman, not on its own. Another old line says it: everything shines after that one shining, even this little fire. Many teachers read arti this way: a small flame is light offered back to where light comes from. Then it leaves the shrine and goes to the people, and each person draws its warmth to their eyes: the same fire for every face. Often prasad follows: food offered to God, handed back as a blessing. Whatever shines in you, a gift, a good day, a win, the old answer is the same. It's borrowed light. Offer it back, then share it.
screen: `ARTI — THE OFFERING OF LIGHT` · `FIRE COULDN'T BURN ONE BLADE OF GRASS` · `EVERYTHING SHINES AFTER THAT ONE` · `THE SAME FIRE TOUCHES EVERY FACE`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. If there's a candle or a lamp near you, look at it; any light in the room will do. Cup your hands toward it, as if gathering warmth, and bring them to your eyes and forehead. Then bring one person to mind and turn your cupped hands toward them, as if passing the plate.
Arti. The offering of light, and then the light shared with everyone. Fifth word.
Your line: light passed hand to hand. Next time the plate comes around, you'll know what you're doing. Day five.

story.title: the blade of grass
story.text: After a great victory, the gods grow proud. A mysterious being appears. Agni, the fire god, boasts he can burn anything; he can't burn the single blade of grass it sets before him. The wind god can't move it. When Indra comes near, the being vanishes, and the goddess Uma tells him it was Brahman, whose victory it had been all along.

6.title: why so many gods?
6.hook: a sage is asked how many gods there are and counts down from 3,306 to one
6.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep images of several deities; many families have a chosen deity (ishta devata) and a family deity, and devotion ranges from one god held as supreme to many honored together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: arti, light passed hand to hand. Today, the question every Hindu kid gets asked at school.

Someone at school or work asks it, half curious, half teasing: how many gods do you have? Ganesha on the dashboard, Krishna in the calendar, Durga at Navratri, Lakshmi at Diwali, a whole shelf at your grandparents' place. It's a fair question. And someone asked it once before, out loud, in front of a king. First, a guess.
screen: `HOW MANY GODS DO YOU HAVE?` → `A FAIR QUESTION.` → `ASKED ONCE BEFORE A KING.`

segments.voice: At a great debate in a king's court, a scholar named Shakalya pressed the sage Yajnavalkya: how many gods are there? Three thousand three hundred and six, Yajnavalkya said, giving the old count. Yes, but how many, really? Thirty-three. How many, really? Six. Three. Two. One and a half. And finally: one. Which one? The breath of life, he said, which the sages call Brahman. Each time, the bigger number folds into the smaller, until only one is left. An even older verse says it in five words: ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti. Truth is one; the wise call it by many names. That's how a lot of Hindus answer the question. The many gods are many faces and names of one reality, the way one person can be a mother, a boss and a friend. Not every Hindu puts it the same way. Some families give their whole devotion to Vishnu, or Shiva, or the Goddess, and see the others within that one. Some honor many, each for a part of life. And almost everyone has an ishta devata: a chosen deity, the form of God that feels like yours. Often it comes from your family; sometimes you find your own. The worry that the others will be upset if you love one most? Faces of one truth don't compete. So the answer at school can be simple: one truth, many names, and one of them feels like home.
screen: `HOW MANY GODS, REALLY? ONE.` · `TRUTH IS ONE; MANY NAMES.` · `MANY FACES OF ONE REALITY.` · `THE ONE THAT FEELS LIKE YOURS.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Think of the image of God you saw most growing up: on a wall, a dashboard, a shelf. Breathe in. As you breathe out, say its name once, quietly, as if it were the name of someone who knows you.
Ishta devata. Your chosen deity: the form of God that feels like yours. Sixth word.
Your line: one truth, many names. Next time someone asks how many gods you have, you've got an answer. Day six.

7.title: not fate, not payback
7.hook: a robber asks if his family will share his deeds; what karma really means
7.tomorrow: what your grandmother was actually doing
7.howItsDone: Hindu teachers speak of karma as action and its fruit, within this life and across lifetimes; schools of thought differ on how karma works and on how a person is freed from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: one truth, many names, and the one that's yours. Six words so far: Ganesha, om, Gayatri, namaste, arti, ishta devata. Today, the seventh.
screen: `GANESHA · OM · GAYATRI · NAMASTE · ARTI · ISHTA DEVATA`

segments.voice: Karma. Someone says it when the car that cut them off gets stuck at the next light. Used like that, it means payback: the universe keeping score. The older meaning turns the whole thing around, and a well-loved story shows how. Long before he was a poet, the story goes, Valmiki was a robber on a forest road. One day he stopped a wandering sage, who asked him a question. You rob to feed your family. Will they share what your deeds bring you? The robber went home and asked. One by one, they said no. What you do is yours. He came back shaken, sat down to meditate, and sat so long that an anthill grew over him. The story says that's where his name comes from: valmika, an anthill. The robber became the poet of the Ramayana.
screen: `KARMA.` → `A ROBBER ON A FOREST ROAD.` → `WHAT YOU DO IS YOURS.` → `FROM ROBBER TO POET.`

segments.voice: Karma is the Sanskrit word for action. A deed. Something done. Krishna teaches that no one can stay without acting, even for a moment: breathing, speaking, choosing, all of it is action. So karma isn't something that happens to you. It's what you do. And what does action do back? One of the oldest Hindu texts says it like a proverb: as a person acts, so that person becomes. Not: so the person is punished. Becomes. Patience, practiced, makes a patient person. Sharpness, practiced, makes a sharp one. That's what the robber learned: no one could carry his deeds for him, and no one could stop him from changing them. The payback version keeps your eyes on other people. The older version turns you around: what am I becoming with my next word? Hindu teachers also speak of karma across lifetimes; that's a bigger conversation for later. For today: as you act, so you become.
screen: `KARMA — ACTION, A DEED` · `AS ONE ACTS, SO ONE BECOMES` · `NO ONE CARRIES YOUR DEEDS` · `WHAT AM I BECOMING?`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Bring to mind one small thing you did this week: a kind word, a sharp one, a promise kept or skipped. Don't grade it. Just ask what it's growing. Then pick one small action you'd be glad to see grow.
Karma. Action, and what action makes of the one who does it. Not payback. Seventh word: a week's worth.
Your line: what you do, you become. That's week one: seven words, and what's inside each. Tomorrow, what your grandmother was actually doing.
